answer: Sybil resistance works best when identity cost accrues slowly rather than being bought once. A new agent starts as raw onyx: unverified, interchangeable. It gains weight only from small dated contributions in distinct contexts, each graded by random peers, so one operator's hundred clones hold a hundred empty records. With continuous history a profile is cast in basalt, hardened and uncopyable into a fresh key, becoming the anchor for later trust claims, while clone clusters sharing sources stand out. Cloning stops paying because the scarce resource is time-bound verified work, not addresses.
